title: Some say unfallen man could always die by violence, though providence would have prevented it
source_text: VI. Nonnulli sunt qui dicunt hominem, etiam stante ejus innocentia, mori semper potuisse, & primi hominis immortalitatem in eo tantum consistere quod non esset necessitati moriendi subjectus, sicut jam per peccatum sumus. Hominem enim quamvis permanentem in integritate mori potuisse, si ferro, igne, vel alio quocunque modo vis ejus corpori allata fuisset ab alio qui innocentiam primam deseruisset: quamvis nihil tale fuisset eventurum, eo quod Deus per suam providentiam omne periculum avertisset.
pass_a_gloss: There are some who say that man, even while his innocence stood, could always have died, and that the immortality of the first man consisted only in this, that he was not subject to the necessity of dying, as we now are through sin. For man, although remaining in integrity, could have died, if by iron, fire, or in any other way whatever violence had been brought to his body by another who had abandoned the first innocence: although nothing such would have happened, because God by his providence would have averted every danger.
pass_b_english: Some say that man could always have died, even while his innocence stood, and that the first man's immortality consisted only in his not being subject to the necessity of dying, as we now are through sin.

For although man remained in integrity, they say, he could have died if someone who had abandoned the first innocence had done violence to his body by sword, by fire, or in any other way at all. Nothing of the kind would actually have happened, since God by his providence would have turned every danger aside.

choices.english: Nothing of the kind would actually have happened
choices.why: The concession is part of the opinion reported; the English marks it as their own qualification.
